1:
The title does not describe the chapter. Adam Clarke observes that by it the prophecy should relate only to Damascus, but treats more largely of Samaria and the Israelites, and that the last three verses are a distinct piece, worked up with great elegance, on the sudden overthrow of Sennacherib. Keil and Delitzsch explain why Israel is drawn in: the curse falls on the northern kingdom too, because it had allied itself with heathen Damascus against its own brother tribe and the Davidic government, and by that alliance with a stranger had become a stranger itself.

The occasion is dated from the earlier confederacy. Charles Ellicott recalls Syria's confederacy with Ephraim against Judah under Ahaz, the prophet then foretelling its overthrow by Assyria, a prediction partly fulfilled already; writing early in Hezekiah's reign, he looks to a further fulfilment. John Wesley assigns the fulfilment to Tiglath-pileser, the city being afterwards rebuilt. John Calvin gives the pastoral reason: the Jews, unable to contend with the Syrian king and stripped of aid, might doubt whether God had abandoned them, and the threat frees them from that doubt.

Then a place-name nobody can place. Clarke protests that Aroer on the Arnon has nothing to do with Damascus, that a second Aroer on Gad's northern border is little better, and that the cities of Aroer makes no sense if Aroer is a city; the Greek read the consonants as for ever, the old paraphrase as a verb meaning they shall be wasted, the Syriac differently again, so the reading is doubtful; he follows the Greek. John Gill keeps the city, given to Reuben and Gad and later taken by the Syrians, and reports a father of the church saw it on a mountain top. Calvin makes it a country rather than a town.

On the third verse textual and political readings part company. Gill takes the fortress for Samaria, or all their strongholds, and cites the paraphrase that the government shall cease from Ephraim, so they should have no more a king, nor have they to this day. Clarke prefers a conjecture reading pride for remnant, the sentence seeming to require something answering to the glory of Israel, and notes eight manuscripts and ten editions read in the glory. Wesley makes the survivors a headless body, and turns the comparison into a levelling: Syria shall have as much glory as Israel, which is to say neither shall have any.

The thinning of Jacob is read as emaciation, then as harvest. Ellicott notes the word is the one rendered impoverished elsewhere, Jacob standing here for the northern kingdom; on the reaper he admires the prophet's habit of localising his imagery, the valley named lying south-west of Jerusalem, famous for fertility and often raided, the prophet having watched a reaper and seen a parable of the invader. Gill has the reaper gather the corn into one hand and cut it with the other, Israel a field of corn for number and beauty. Calvin says the metaphor was chosen because a people trusting its numbers dreads nothing, though no reaper is daunted by the quantity of corn.

The gleaning is the one relief, its beneficiaries disputed. Calvin marks the change of sense: having said nothing would be left, the prophet abates the severity, since grapes are never gleaned so closely that none stay hidden under the leaves, nor an olive shaken so thoroughly that none remain on top. Matthew Henry calls it mercy reserved in a parenthesis in the midst of judgment, the meek hidden in the day of anger and comfortable in Judah, where they had the liberty of God's courts. Ellicott sees the remnant idea held even for the northern kingdom, vineyard then olive-yard supplying the figure. Gill reports rabbis referring the few instead to Jerusalem, to Hezekiah's company, or to survivors of the Assyrian army.
7:
The turn to the Maker is warning as much as promise. Charles Ellicott says there is to be a return to the true faith, brought about by bitter experience of the results of idolatry. John Calvin calls it the fruit of the chastisement, a second consolation for the godly, adding that when men betake themselves to God the disordered world returns to its proper order. John Gill takes the man for the remnant according to the election of grace, and directs the looking to Christ, the Maker of all things, for righteousness and salvation.

The altars are a knot of grammar before a rebuke. Adam Clarke says the construction is not obvious and that all the ancient versions and most modern ones have mistaken it: the word for work governs the word for altars rather than standing beside it, so the sense is the altars of the work of their hands, the idols. Gill reports the rabbi Clarke follows, who separated the clauses because otherwise all altars, even God's, were works of men yet right to look to. Ellicott identifies the objects: conical tree-like pillars symbolising a Canaanite goddess, and sun-images. Calvin draws the doctrine, that the looking of the previous verse means hope and confidence, and that no one sees God clearly without driving off every superstition.

Then the text collapses. Clarke says no one has made any tolerable sense of the two words, that the Greek preserves what seems the true reading, the Amorites and the Hivites, and that many who would never admit the Greek reading nonetheless expound the verse of that very event. Ellicott renders it a forsaken tract of forest and hill-top, the usual fortress sites, and grants the Greek either followed another reading or paraphrased curiously. Calvin calls the view that the words are names of towns forced, taking them for disagreeable places, so that walls and ditches would defend no better than thickets.

The picture itself is agreed. Gill has the cities forsaken like a bough stripped of its leaves. Matthew Henry presses that the strong cities which should have protected the country cannot protect themselves, and will look like an old tree's top branch, bare and dry and dead. Wesley notes the pruner neglects the uppermost branch as useless, and that the Canaanites forsook their cities for fear of Israel — a fit example, since God had inflicted the same judgment for the same sins.

The cause is stated plainly. Calvin says the reason is given so they may not complain of injustice: the evils come because they wickedly despised God, an inexcusable ingratitude that prostituted their hopes to heathen nations and idols as if they had never known his love. Gill lists the salvations forgotten: Egypt, the Red Sea and since. Ellicott finds the retribution exact, the rock of their strength contrasted with the rock-fortresses they trusted: they had forsaken the One, so the others should be forsaken.

The foreign planting is where readings diverge. Ellicott would render thou didst plant, notes the word for pleasant occurs here only as a common noun and elsewhere as a personal name, most familiarly a Syrian general's, and infers the prophet chose it to mark the planting as Syrian, comparing the alliance's rapid growth to the gardens grown for a dying god. Clarke reads the shoots from foreign soil allegorically, for idolatrous worship and reliance on foreign alliances. Wesley keeps them literal: flowers and fruit-trees fetched from far countries and highly esteemed. Keil and Delitzsch print the planting and the woe against the nations as one movement. Calvin finds the next verse ambiguous, rejecting the rendering about removing a branch on the day of affliction, and takes the disputed noun in its plain sense of produce; Gill and Wesley agree the point is unsparing diligence, day after day from earliest morning, ending in one heap.
12:
Everyone notices that the chapter has changed hands. Adam Clarke says the last three verses seem to have no relation to the prophecy they are joined to, nor to what follows, a beautiful piece standing singly by itself, and he cannot say whether it stands in its right place; it is a noble description of the invasion and sudden overthrow of Sennacherib, in the strongest and most expressive images. Charles Ellicott agrees it is an isolated fragment, probably placed here because it opens like the next chapter, and suggests the parallel with the harvest of grief just before may have prompted the insertion. John Gill says a new subject is begun, though a short one; John Wesley calls it a new prophecy added for the comfort of God's people.

Who is meant, and in what tone, is less agreed. Gill rules out two readings, that the prophet bemoans the Jews with Hezekiah and that the multitude is Syria and Israel combined, and settles on Sennacherib's army, drawn from many nations and very numerous. John Calvin turns to the interjection: some render it execration and it is sometimes a call to a person, but he thinks it betokens sorrow, the prophet groaning over the calamity he foresees, out of brotherly affection or to press the threat on a sluggish people. The prophets, he adds, regarded God's vengeance with greater horror than other men, and though they threatened severely they never laid aside human feeling so as not to pity those who perished.

Matthew Henry reads the passage as the doom of those who spoil and rob the people of God. They relied on their numbers, an army made up of divers nations, by whose weight they hoped to carry the cause; they were noisy as the roaring seas, talking big and threatening to frighten God's people from resisting and their allies from sending aid, Sennacherib and his officer making a mighty noise in speeches and letters to strike terror into Hezekiah. Ellicott notes that the rushing of mighty waters for an army's march has its parallel in an earlier chapter.

Two of them stop to weigh the words. Clarke reports that five, three ending one verse and two beginning the next, are omitted by eight manuscripts and the Syriac, so the repetition is not made; and in the last verse he prefers a particle attested by many good vouchers which restores the true poetical form, at the season of evening behold terror, before the morning and behold he is no more, adding that manuscripts and the Syriac read the singular, him that spoileth us, which answers better to Sennacherib. Ellicott would drop the supplied word God, since it weakens the sublime indefiniteness of the Hebrew, and identifies the rolling thing with the wheel of a psalm, dust-clouds whirling from an elevated threshing-floor, denying any authority for the margin's thistle-down.

The suddenness is where the consolation lies. Calvin insists the comfort is not for the Jews only, since the discourse has been addressed to the ten tribes, among whom some still feared God and would have despaired without a promise; his image is a storm raised at sea and soon allayed, leaving no trace, prosperity arising contrary to expectation. Two things are stated, that the attack will be sudden and that the ravages will not last: tyrants rush upon us like whirlwinds, but the Lord easily dispels their rage. Gill takes the trouble at eveningtide of Hezekiah and Jerusalem on the night before deliverance, with the land wasted and the enemy blaspheming, though he reports others who place the terror in the Assyrian camp and a rabbi who makes it the work of demons. Ellicott says the words, general as they are, were specially fulfilled in the destruction of that army. Keil and Delitzsch print the closing verses without a word of comment.
